title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: "Come, it's all over, and thank God!" was the first thought that came to Anna Arkadyevna when she had said good-bye for the last time to her brother, who had stood blocking up the entrance to the carriage until the third bell rang. She sat down on her seat beside Annushka and looked around her in the twilight of the sleeping car. "Thank God! Tomorrow I'll see Seryozha and Alexey Alexandrovitch, and my life will go on as it used to, all nice and the same as always."

Still in the same anxious frame of mind she had been in all day, Anna took pleasure in arranging herself for the journey with great care. With her little deft hands she opened and shut her little red bag, took out a cushion, laid it on her knees, and, carefully wrapping up her feet, settled herself comfortably. An invalid lady had already lain down to sleep. Two other ladies began talking to Anna, and a stout elderly lady tucked up her feet and made remarks about the heating of the train. Anna answered them in a few words, but not foreseeing any entertainment from the conversation, she asked Annushka to get her a lamp, hooked it onto the arm of her seat, and took from her bag a paper-knife and an English novel. At first her reading made no progress. The fuss and bustle were distracting; then, once the train had started, she could not help listening to the noises; then the snow beating on the left window and sticking to the pane, and the sight of the muffled guard going by, covered with snow on one side, and the conversations about the terrible snowstorm raging outside, all distracted her. Farther on, it was the same thing over and over: the same shaking and rattling, the same snow on the window, the same rapid switches from steaming heat to cold and back again to heat, the same passing glimpses of the same figures in the twilight, the same voices, and Anna began to read and to take in what she was reading. Annushka was already dozing, the red bag on her lap, clutched by her broad gloved hands, one of the gloves torn. Anna Arkadyevna read and understood, but it was distasteful to her to read, that is, to follow the reflection of other people's lives. She wanted too much to live herself. If she read that the heroine of the novel was nursing a sick man, she longed to be moving with noiseless steps about the room of a sick man; if she read of a member of Parliament making a speech, she longed to be making the speech herself; if she read of how Lady Mary had ridden after the hounds and provoked her sister-in-law and surprised everyone by her boldness, she too wished to be doing the same. But there was no chance of doing anything; and twisting the smooth paper-knife in her little hands, she forced herself to read.

The hero of the novel was already on the verge of his English happiness, a baronetcy and an estate, and Anna was feeling a wish to go with him to the estate, when she suddenly felt that _he_ ought to be ashamed, and that she was ashamed of the same thing. But what did he have to be ashamed of? "What do I have to be ashamed of?" she asked herself, surprised and hurt. She put the book down and sank against the back of the chair, gripping the paper-cutter tightly in both hands. There was nothing. She went over all her Moscow memories. They were all good, pleasant. She remembered the ball, remembered Vronsky and his face of slavish adoration, remembered all her behavior with him: there was nothing shameful. And yet, at the same point in her memories, the feeling of shame grew sharper, as though some inner voice, just at the point when she thought of Vronsky, were saying to her, "Warm, very warm, hot." "Well, what is it?" she said to herself resolutely, shifting her position. "What does it mean? Am I afraid to look it straight in the face? Why, what is it? Can it be that between me and this officer boy there exist, or can ever exist, any relations other than those one has with any acquaintance?" She laughed contemptuously and picked up her book again, but now she was utterly unable to follow what she was reading. She drew the paper-knife along the windowpane, then laid its smooth, cool surface against her cheek, and almost laughed aloud from the feeling of delight that suddenly came over her without cause. She felt as though her nerves were strings being tightened on some sort of screwing peg. She felt her eyes opening wider and wider, her fingers and toes twitching nervously, something inside oppressing her breathing, while all shapes and sounds, in the uncertain half-light, struck her with unaccustomed vividness. Moments of doubt kept coming over her, when she was not sure whether the train was going forward or backward, or standing still altogether; whether it was Annushka at her side or a stranger. "What's that on the arm of the chair, a fur cloak or some beast? And what am I myself? Am I myself or some other woman?" She was afraid of giving way to this delirium. But something drew her toward it, and she could yield to it or resist it at will. She got up to rouse herself, took off her plaid and the cape of her warm dress. For a moment she regained her self-possession and realized that the thin peasant who had come in wearing a long overcoat with buttons missing was the stoveheater, that he was looking at the thermometer, that it was the wind and snow bursting in after him at the door; but then everything grew blurred again... That peasant with the long waist seemed to be gnawing something on the wall; the old lady began stretching her legs the whole length of the carriage and filling it with a black cloud; then there was a terrible shrieking and banging, as if someone were being torn to pieces; then a blinding dazzle of red fire before her eyes, and a wall seemed to rise up and hide everything. Anna felt as though she were sinking down. But it was not terrible; it was delightful. The voice of a man muffled up and covered with snow shouted something in her ear. She got up and pulled herself together; she realized that they had reached a station and that this was the guard. She asked Annushka to hand her the cape she had taken off and her shawl, put them on, and moved toward the door.
"Do you want to get out?" asked Annushka.

"Yes, I'd like a little air. It's so hot in here." And she opened the door. The driving snow and the wind rushed to meet her and wrestled with her over the door. But she found she was enjoying the struggle.

She opened the door and stepped out. The wind seemed to have been lying in wait for her; with a gleeful whistle it tried to snatch her up and carry her off, but she clung to the cold doorpost, and, holding her skirt, got down onto the platform and into the shelter of the carriages. The wind had been powerful on the steps, but on the platform, in the lee of the carriages, there was a lull. With enjoyment she drew in deep breaths of the freezing, snowy air, and standing by the carriage, she looked around at the platform and the lit-up station.
